analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug payments at the lowest price the federal government already pays.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. Sanders with one Democratic cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what Medicare pays for prescription drugs under Parts B and D at the lower of what the Department of Veterans Affairs or the federal supply schedule pays for the same drug, roughly half or less of current Medicare prices. Drug makers would have to agree to sell at that price for Medicare coverage to continue. The bill never advanced past a committee referral in the 117th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and, indirectly, all drug purchasers, because the government would pay prices closer to those other federal agencies already pay, reducing drug spending and cost-sharing; taxpayers would save on Medicare drug outlays.
analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would have to sell to Medicare at federal procurement prices, roughly half current levels, or lose Medicare coverage for their drugs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action before the 117th Congress ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept higher prices

sides.party_line_note: Only Sen. Sanders and one Democratic cosponsor supported the bill; no recorded opposition or votes occurred.
